stem: Early experiments were interpreted as showing "normal left ventricular function" after hours of CPB with the heart **perfused, empty and beating**. According to current information, which finding shows this method is **not ideal**?

choices.text: Phrenic nerve palsy from cold saline placed in the pericardium
Prolonged electromechanical quiescence after the heart is reperfused
Myocardial water accumulation that reduces ventricular distensibility
Coronary sinus rupture during insertion of the perfusion catheter
Coronary air embolization each time coronary perfusion is resumed

explanation.text: With the heart perfused, empty and beating, **water accumulates in the myocardium** during CPB; in dog models ventricular **distensibility fell by nearly 50%** after 3 hours.

items: **Myocardial water** accumulates -> ventricular distensibility ↓ (nearly 50% after 3 h, dog models)
**Distribution of coronary blood** is abnormal
Changed myocardial compressive forces and LV wall geometry **impede intracoronary collateral flow** to potentially ischemic areas

explanation.title: Still useful when used properly
explanation.text: The method can serve well for various procedures and is often combined with **mild or moderate hypothermia**; McGoon and colleagues reported **100 consecutive isolated aortic valve replacements** with this method and **no hospital deaths**.

explanation.title: Not damage-free
explanation.text: CPB itself, with the heart perfused and beating empty, already produces some damage.

Water tends to accumulate in the myocardium during CPB; as a result, ventricular distensibility in dog models is decreased by nearly 50% after 3 hours of CPB with the heart perfused, empty, and beating.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 96

choiceNotes.a: Phrenic nerve palsy is linked to filling the pericardium with very cold saline in **profoundly hypothermic global ischemia**.
choiceNotes.b: Prolonged electromechanical quiescence is a drawback of **verapamil and diltiazem** in cardioplegic solutions.
choiceNotes.d: Coronary sinus rupture is a complication of **retrograde cardioplegia**.
choiceNotes.e: Repeated coronary air embolization is a drawback of **moderately hypothermic intermittent ischemia**.

stem: An 82-year-old man with **extensive arteriosclerosis of the aorta** needs CABG. Which approach, combined with the perfused empty beating heart, has been reported to **reduce intraoperative and postoperative strokes** in such patients?

choices.text: Profound hypothermia with cold pericardial saline and one clamp period
Intermittent aortic clamping for 10–15 minutes at 25°C–30°C
Cold antegrade cardioplegia through an aortic root catheter
Electrical fibrillation just before each period of aortic clamping
Both ITAs with stabilizers, no aortic clamp, and axillary cannulation

explanation.text: In elderly patients or those with **extensive aortic arteriosclerosis**, CABG with **both internal thoracic arteries**, **stabilizers**, **no aortic clamping** ("no-touch") and CPB by **peripheral cannulation** (e.g., axillary artery) reduces intraoperative and postoperative strokes.

explanation.center: **No-touch** CABG on the empty beating heart

explanation.title: Why it helps
explanation.text: Tarakji and colleagues report that this technique, **without aortic clamping**, reduces **intraoperative and postoperative strokes** in such patients.
in elderly patients or those with extensive arteriosclerosis of the aorta, CABG using both internal thoracic arteries may be performed using stabilizers
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 96

choiceNotes.a: Profound hypothermic global ischemia requires **clamping the aorta**, and pericardial cold saline causes phrenic nerve palsy.
choiceNotes.b: Intermittent ischemia clamps the aorta repeatedly; this is the opposite of the no-touch approach.
choiceNotes.c: An aortic root catheter and cardioplegia need an **aortic clamp**; the no-touch technique avoids clamping.
choiceNotes.d: Electrical fibrillation before each clamp period is part of **moderately hypothermic intermittent ischemia**, which clamps the aorta repeatedly; the reported technique uses **no aortic clamping**.

stem: During aortic valve replacement on the perfused empty beating heart, small cannulae are placed in the right and left coronary ostia. In about **50% of patients**, which region is **not perfused** by the cannula in the right coronary ostium?

choices.text: The right ventricular infundibulum, via a separately arising conus artery
The circumflex territory, when the tip passes the left main bifurcation
The left ventricular subendocardium, during persistent fibrillation
The anterior descending territory, from its separate aortic origin
The right atrium and right ventricular midportion, via the coronary sinus

explanation.text: In about **50%** of patients the **conus artery**, which supplies the **infundibulum of the right ventricle**, arises **separately from the aortic sinus**, so a right coronary ostial cannula does not perfuse it.

explanation.caption: Why individual coronary cannulation is imperfect
head: Problem
Consequence
rows: Cannula tip beyond the **left main bifurcation**
Only the LAD **or** circumflex is perfused
RV infundibulum not perfused by the right ostial cannula
May be difficult in certain cases

explanation.title: Right vs left problem
explanation.text: Tip position past the bifurcation is a **left** cannula problem; the **conus artery** is the **right** cannula problem.

In about 50% of patients, the conus artery supplying the infundibulum of the right ventricle arises separately from the aortic sinus and is not perfused by a cannula inserted into the right coronary ostium.

choiceNotes.b: Passing the left main bifurcation is a problem of the **left** ostial cannula, not the right one.
choiceNotes.c: Subendocardial underperfusion relates to ventricular fibrillation, not to the right ostial cannula missing a vessel in half of patients.
choiceNotes.d: Separate LAD and circumflex origins occur in about **1%**, and concern the left system.
choiceNotes.e: Poorer perfusion of the RA and RV midportion is a feature of **retrograde coronary sinus** cardioplegia.

stem: A 58-year-old man with aortic stenosis from a **congenitally bicuspid valve** is to undergo aortic valve replacement with **individual coronary artery perfusion**. Why may proper left coronary cannulation be **more difficult** than usual in this patient?

choices.text: The conus artery arises separately from the aortic sinus
Subendocardial flow is impaired by ventricular hypertrophy
Right dominance is more common, with a longer left main
Left dominance is more common, with a shorter left main
Blood leaking around the cannulae forces pauses in perfusion

explanation.text: In aortic stenosis due to a **congenitally bicuspid valve**, **left dominant** systems are more prevalent than normal, and in left dominant systems the **left main coronary artery is shorter**, making individual left coronary perfusion more difficult.

explanation.title: Bicuspid AS and the left cannula
General vs patient-specific
explanation.text: Leakage around cannulae and the separate conus artery affect individual perfusion in many patients; the **bicuspid-specific** problem is the **short left main** of left dominance.

The prevalence of left dominant systems in patients with aortic stenosis secondary to congenital bicuspid valves is higher than normal; in left dominant systems, the left main coronary artery is shorter than normal

choiceNotes.a: A separate conus artery (about 50% of patients) affects perfusion through the **right** ostial cannula, not left cannulation.
choiceNotes.b: Impaired subendocardial perfusion in hypertrophy is described for **ventricular fibrillation** during CPB, not for cannulation difficulty.
choiceNotes.c: The source states the opposite: **left** dominance is more prevalent, and the left main is **shorter**.
choiceNotes.e: Leakage around the cannulae can interrupt perfusion in any patient; it does not explain the bicuspid-specific difficulty.

Mechanical injury to the coronary ostia by the cannulae
Coronary perfusion flow of 300 mL per minute

steps.text: Cannulae placed directly into the **coronary ostia**

stem: When the empty heart is perfused through **individual coronary cannulae** during aortic valve surgery, which perfusate temperature is advised, and why?

choices.text: Warmer than 30°C, so the heart keeps beating instead of fibrillating
25°C–30°C, so fibrillation is maintained by hypothermia alone
37°C, with fibrillation maintained by an electrical current
About 22°C, with very cold saline added to the pericardium
33°C–34°C, so the aorta can be clamped before fibrillation

explanation.text: With this method the heart should be **kept beating**, so the perfusate should be **warmer than 30°C**.

steps.label: result
steps.text: Higher risk of perioperative **infarction and death** than with a beating heart (Spanos and colleagues)

explanation.title: Don't mix up the temperatures
explanation.text: **25°C–30°C** sustains fibrillation (hypothermic fibrillating heart); **33°C–34°C** is the CPB temperature before cardioplegia; **warmer than 30°C** keeps the individually perfused heart beating.
When this method is used, the heart should be kept beating; therefore, the perfusate should be warmer than 30°C.

choiceNotes.b: 25°C–30°C coronary perfusion sustains **fibrillation** (the hypothermic fibrillating heart method); here the heart should be beating.
choiceNotes.c: Electrically maintained fibrillation at 37°C belongs to the **fibrillating heart** method; persistent fibrillation raised infarction and death risk here.
choiceNotes.d: About 22°C is the myocardial temperature of **profoundly hypothermic global ischemia**.
choiceNotes.e: 33°C–34°C is the perfusate temperature at the start of CPB before **antegrade cardioplegia**.

stem: A surgeon plans CABG with **continuous coronary perfusion through the intact aortic root** and a **fibrillating heart**. Which statement about this method is correct?

choices.text: At 37°C perfusion, fibrillation persists without an electrical current
Fibrillation maintained by 25°C–30°C perfusion is the desirable form
Subendocardial perfusion is best preserved in hypertrophied ventricles
Its safe time limits have been clearly defined in clinical series
Most surgeons find its operating conditions better than cardioplegia

explanation.text: Fibrillation spontaneously or electrically induced and **maintained by moderately hypothermic (25°C–30°C) coronary perfusion** is the desirable condition; at **37°C** an **electrical current** is needed to maintain it.

explanation.caption: Fibrillating heart: what the source says
head: Point
Source
rows: **Impaired** during CPB and VF, especially with **hypertrophy**
Better than the beating heart, **less satisfactory** than cardioplegia

explanation.title: Hypertrophy
explanation.text: The hypertrophied ventricle is the one whose **subendocardium** is most at risk during fibrillation.
The surgical conditions that exist with this method are better than with the beating heart, but most surgeons find them less satisfactory than with a cardioplegic technique.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 96

choiceNotes.a: At 37°C fibrillation must be maintained by an **electrical current**.
choiceNotes.c: Subendocardial perfusion is **impaired** during CPB and fibrillation, **particularly** in hypertrophied ventricles.
choiceNotes.d: Time constraints must apply, but the source says they **have not been defined**.
choiceNotes.e: Most surgeons find conditions **less satisfactory** than with a cardioplegic technique (though better than the beating heart).

stem: Which protocol describes **moderately hypothermic intermittent global myocardial ischemia**?

choices.text: Perfusate 33°C–34°C; clamp 20 min; release 1–2 min with the heart arrested
Perfusate 25°C–30°C; clamp 30–40 min; release 10–20 min with the heart fibrillating
Myocardium near 22°C; a single clamp period for the whole operation
Perfusate 25°C–30°C; clamp 10–15 min; release 3–5 min with the heart beating
Perfusate 25°C–30°C; clamp 10–15 min; release 3–5 min with the heart fibrillating

steps.label: clamp aorta
steps.text: Work on or in the heart **10–15 min** (no coronary perfusion)

explanation.title: Beat, not fibrillate
explanation.text: Used optimally, the heart is made to **beat** during the reperfusion interval.

choiceNotes.c: A single clamp period with myocardium near 22°C is **profoundly hypothermic global ischemia**.

stem: Moderately hypothermic intermittent ischemia gives reasonable working conditions for CABG. Which drawback does the source attribute to **repeatedly resuming coronary perfusion** with this method?

choices.text: Phrenic nerve palsy from cold saline in the pericardium
Potent negative inotropy with prolonged electrical quiescence
Maldistribution of perfusate to the right ventricle
Ventricular distensibility reduced by nearly half
Coronary air embolization and a reperfusion injury each time

explanation.text: Each time coronary perfusion is recommenced, **coronary (and perhaps systemic) air embolization** may occur, and each uncontrolled reperfusion may cause a **reperfusion injury**.

items: Not optimal exposure for **intracardiac** operations (reasonable for CABG)
Heart keeps **beating** during much of the ischemic period unless electrically fibrillated before clamping -> precise repair difficult
**Air embolization** each time perfusion restarts
Blood entering the heart **stresses suckers** -> more blood damage, less smooth operation
**Reperfusion injury** with each uncontrolled reperfusion

explanation.title: Evidence of damage
explanation.text: In McGoon's analysis of **468** patients receiving valved extracardiac conduits, there was no relationship between non-survivors and cumulative clamp time, but **35%** had low cardiac output (mortality **52%** in that subset), so the method **must have been producing myocardial damage**.
Moreover, each time the coronary arteries are perfused in this uncontrolled manner, a reperfusion injury may occur.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 97

choiceNotes.a: Phrenic nerve palsy follows very cold saline in the pericardium in **profoundly hypothermic** ischemia.
choiceNotes.b: Negative inotropy and prolonged quiescence are attributed to **verapamil and diltiazem** in cardioplegic solutions.
choiceNotes.c: Right ventricular maldistribution is a disadvantage of **retrograde cardioplegia**.
choiceNotes.d: Reduced distensibility from myocardial water is described for the **perfused empty beating heart**.

stem: A randomized study compared **profoundly hypothermic global ischemia** with **continuous individual coronary artery perfusion** in patients undergoing **aortic valve replacement**. What did it show about myocardial necrosis?

choices.text: Far less necrosis with cold ischemic arrest
Far less necrosis with individual coronary perfusion
As much necrosis with either technique
No measurable necrosis with either technique
Necrosis only when the perfused heart fibrillated

explanation.text: A randomized study of patients undergoing AVR showed that profoundly hypothermic global ischemia results in **as much myocardial necrosis** as continuous individual coronary perfusion (p. 97).

head: Finding
Proportion
rows: Compared with patients randomly assigned to **cold ischemic arrest**

They are potent negative inotropes causing prolonged quiescence

Intermittent ischemia; as a nucleotide transport inhibitor

stem: Why is **del Nido cardioplegia** considered especially suited to **pediatric** cardiac surgery?

choices.text: Its high calcium content supports the immature myofilaments
It is redosed every 20 minutes to protect immature hearts
It limits sodium and calcium influx into immature myocardium
A simple hyperkalemic blood solution without lidocaine
Its blood-rich mixture avoids hemodilution in small patients

explanation.text: Del Nido solution (**lidocaine**, histidine, **low calcium**, plus potassium and adenosine) **limits sodium and calcium influx** into myocytes, which suits **immature myocardium**, especially susceptible to **reperfusion injury**.

children: Immature myocardium prone to reperfusion injury
No redosing for up to **90 min**

explanation.title: Ratio
explanation.text: In adult comparisons del Nido was used at a **1:4 ratio of blood to crystalloid**; to avoid **hemodilution**, hemoconcentration has been recommended.
This limitation of sodium and calcium influx into the cardiac myocytes is especially suited for pediatric cardiac surgery, as immature myocardium is especially susceptible to reperfusion injury.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 98

choiceNotes.a: Del Nido solution contains **low** calcium, not high calcium.
choiceNotes.b: A single dose is given **without the need for redosing for up to 90 minutes**.
choiceNotes.d: Lidocaine is one of the **main components** of del Nido solution, with histidine, low calcium, potassium and adenosine.
choiceNotes.e: Its ratio is **1:4 blood to crystalloid**, and hemodilution is a recognized problem needing ultrafiltration or micro del Nido.

stem: A 70-year-old with **low ejection fraction and right ventricular dysfunction** needs a long, complex operation, and del Nido cardioplegia is proposed. Which statement reflects the source's view of del Nido in adults?

choices.text: It has proved clearly superior to other blood cardioplegic solutions
A single dose cannot cover routine isolated CABG or valve operations
Hemodilution is not a concern, so ultrafiltration is rarely used
Evidence is lacking in low-EF and energy-depleted hearts
It has been abandoned in congenital heart surgery

explanation.text: Uncertainties in adults include **safety for prolonged cross-clamp time and when to redose**, and **effectiveness in reduced RV function, low EF and energy-depleted hearts**; some randomized trials have excluded these patients.

items: Prolonged cross-clamp time: is it safe, and **when to redose**?
Reduced **RV function**, **low EF**, **energy-depleted** hearts: lack of evidence
**Second cross-clamp** period needing more cardioplegia: what to do?
**Hemodilution**: hemoconcentration recommended; **ultrafiltration** reported in **83.7%** of del Nido cases; **micro del Nido** suggested

explanation.title: "No difference" ≠ "proven equal everywhere"
explanation.text: Comparisons in adults showed almost no significant differences in most parameters, but many studies used **non-standardized** (modified) solutions and focused on isolated CABG or valve operations, where **one dose suffices**.
Several publications have raised concerns about the lack of evidence for del Nido cardioplegia in these patients, and some randomized trials have excluded them.

choiceNotes.a: Comparisons with other blood-based solutions showed **almost no statistically significant differences** in most parameters.
choiceNotes.b: In isolated CABG or valve operations a **single dose will suffice** for the entire operation.
choiceNotes.c: Ultrafiltration has been reported in **83.7%** of del Nido cases, and hemoconcentration has been recommended.
choiceNotes.e: It has been used extensively in congenital heart surgery at Children's Hospital Boston since 1994.

stem: During cold antegrade cardioplegic induction, the monitored **aortic root pressure is 25 mmHg** while a **left ventricular vent** is running. What should the surgeon do?

Raise both the flow rate and the total cardioplegic dose until pressure exceeds 75 mmHg
Reduce the flow rate, since low pressure means the coronary bed is already filled
Accept the pressure, because flow and dose are set by body surface area alone
Stop the infusion and switch to individual coronary ostial cannulation

explanation.text: If root pressure is **< 30 mmHg**, the **flow rate, but not the total dose,** is increased; but low pressure may be **aortic regurgitation hidden by the LV vent**, and the surgeon must be certain this is not the case.

Action

choiceNotes.b: Only the **flow rate** is increased, **not the total dose**; 75 mmHg is the level sometimes seen in severe ischemic disease, not a target.

stem: During a long operation with intermittent cold antegrade cardioplegia, how are **reinfusions** given?

choices.text: About every 40 min, for 3 min, at half the initial flow
About every 20 min, for 1–2 min, at the initial flow
About every 20 min, for 3 min, at twice the initial flow
Only when electrical activity returns, for 5 min at the initial flow
About every 10 min, for 30 seconds, at the initial flow

explanation.text: Cardioplegic solution is reinfused **about every 20 minutes** for **1 to 2 minutes** at the **initial flow rate**, and the surgeon ensures the **aortic valve has closed** as infusion begins.

items: Interval: **about every 20 min**

Valve not closed? **A few pinches of the proximal aorta** usually close it
